newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.AFRICAN RESERVE BANK DATA - BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.AFRICAN RESERVE BANK DATA - BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
(This week's column by our weekly contributor takes the form of an open letter to Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals.)

You have just broken the mould of tradition by releasing the foreign reserve position of the Reserve Bank days ahead of the publication of the Bank's balance sheet where it would normally have been disclosed.
The explanation given for this departure was the public interest shown in the reserves, not that there was anything new in that. There has always been that interest and, perhaps, unduly so.

There was denial that the early release was triggered by rumoured leaks from within the Bank. Good, but the mounting rumours of leaks from moles in the Bank are perturbing. Just as the new way of making public decisions of Cabinet is to leak the Cabinet minutes, which are marked as Top Secret. This erosion of security standards is worrying.

However, be that as it may, the earlier release of the reserves is altogether welcome. But why should it end there? It has frequently been noted by yourself and other spokesmen of the Bank that the Bank's position is but a part, albeit the major part, of the overall reserve position of the country.

Changes in the overall reserves are the relevant figures in relation to balance of payments transactions. And furthermore, there can be movement between the reserves of the Bank and other units of the monetary system which could account for much of the change in Reserve Bank's reserves. In other words we are getting only part of the picture in having the Bank's figures, which can be misleading.

So why not do the obvious and have the Reserve Bank publish the full reserve position of the monetary system? This would entail the gross reserves fo the Reserve Bank, the foreign loans of the Bank related to reserves and the gross foreign balances of the rest of the monetary system.

I can see no insuperable difficulty here. It would simply entail a collection by phone or fax of the foreign balance of the respective banks making up the rest of the monetary system as at the last day of the month. The banks must have this information available on a daily basis.

The foreign balances of the other banks will also prove to be of great interest in their own right as there is growing acceptance of forward contract risks for which adequate working balances abroad have to be maintained.

As you know the foreign liabilities of the other banks is now conventionally not taken into account in arriving at the net reserves, following the advice to this effect given by the IMF some years ago. Changes to these are entered elsewhere as a balance of payments transaction. This means only a single figure from each bank is required and that could be to the nearest million rand after applying the appropriate end-of-month exchange rates.
In this modern era of transparency going this one step further would be most helpful for a more enlightened public understanding of what is happening.

However, the job would be really well done if the Reserve Bank were to provide additional information in the release from time to time, as relevant, of major factors that the Bank is aware of that have contributed significantly to the movement of the reserves in a month - such as the ECU loan repayment, interest payments on government stock, and redemptions of converted medium-term standstill loans this last February.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
